#3414. Latest Update: How Social Department built culture-aware video discovery

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2275 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How Social Department built culture-aware video discovery

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is co-written by Mariah Miller and Sirajus Salekin from AWS and Nicholas Chase from Social Department.
  • Entertainment marketing teams manage tens of thousands of video assets across studios, networks, and streaming applications.
  • Semantic search, on its own, has a ceiling: It answers the question you can articulate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is co-written by Mariah Miller and Sirajus Salekin from AWS and Nicholas Chase from Social Department.

Entertainment marketing teams manage tens of thousands of video assets across studios, networks, and streaming applications. Most campaigns begin with the same video discovery problem: finding the one moment in the footage that will resonate with an audience. When a brief lands, the clock starts, and what they need is almost never something a database can describe.

Semantic search, on its own, has a ceiling: It answers the question you can articulate. Ask it for a character holding a coffee mug and it will find every coffee mug in a thousand episodes. The queries that actually drive entertainment campaigns look nothing like that. They are questions of judgment: which moment in a show will travel, which line is quotable, and which single frame will work as a meme.

Recent findings suggest that those questions can’t be typed into a search box. Answering them requires two things the search index doesn’t have: an editorial definition of what “quotable” or “memeable” means for a given library, and a continuously refreshed view of what is moving outside the library. Historically, answering them meant a person with deep knowledge of the show watching footage for a week, and that person doesn’t scale across a catalog.

According to recent reports, in this post, we describe how Social Department, the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, set out to encode those editorial questions as executable retrieval pipelines. The result is QuickSearch, a set of single-action queries that return the clips a marketer is looking for without requiring them to describe it: Shareable Scenes, Quotable Quotes, Memeable Moments, and Trend Align.

The models in this solution run on Amazon Bedrock, so customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. It isn’t shared with model providers and isn’t used to train the underlying models.

Industry observers note that social Department’s approach to responsible AI is that AI proposes and people decide. In production, code checks generated output against the source material (for example, a quote is discarded if it isn’t in the episode transcript). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen customer search text for prompt attacks, and a person on the customer’s team approves every post before it publishes.

It has been revealed that social Department owns the pipeline architecture, the retrieval system, and the editorial criteria behind each action. TrackIt, an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner, implemented and delivered against that design. TwelveLabs’ Marengo 3.0 and Pegasus 1.2 models on Amazon Bedrock provide the scene-level video reasoning the pipeline builds on. AWS supplies the infrastructure, the model access including Anthropic’s Claude models, and Amazon OpenSearch Service, using its serverless option, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, for retrieval.

A note on scope: This post describes the AWS portions of the system: the ingest and indexing pipeline, the retrieval path, and the services that run them. The components Social Department owns, including its media and data backbone, content analysis and discovery engine, editorial criteria, and evaluation program, are described only to the depth needed to follow the architecture. The named services that follow are the ones this post is about, not an inventory of Social Department’s full system.

Industry observers note that social Department is the AI operating system for entertainment marketing, serving major studios, networks, streamers, and FAST applications. It automates campaign strategy, asset creation, publishing, and performance optimization across a client’s full content library. Most of those functions depend on locating the right moment inside the footage first, and semantic clip discovery has been core to the product from the beginning.

Entertainment marketing operates under two constraints that a general-purpose search layer can’t satisfy.

According to recent reports, A marketer can describe an object, a location, or a line of dialogue, but not what will travel. That judgment, this moment lands and that one doesn’t, is the actual skill in the job. It was never automatable because it depends on knowing how an audience behaves rather than what a video contains. A search layer that only understands content requires a human to supply the intent, and supplying that intent well requires having already watched the show.

According to recent reports, no amount of video understanding tells you what audiences are talking about this morning. That information is created outside the library and changes hourly, while a library changes only when newly introduced content is added. A system that answers these queries has to acquire trend signal continuously and reconcile it against the library at request time.

That distinction drove the core architectural decision: content understanding and trend acquisition run as independent pipelines on their own schedules and are joined only when a user selects a QuickSearch action.

According to recent reports, with QuickSearch, teams can interact with a video library in a different way, one where the system proposes rather than waits. It provides four actions, each with its own retrieval strategy, editorial criteria, and ranking model. The walkthrough that follows describes how each is implemented. The list here introduces what they do.

Alongside these, Social Department keeps natural-language search for everything the actions don’t cover, and image-based search, where a reference image returns visually similar content across the library.

The following diagram shows how the three parts of the architecture connect. The content understanding pipeline makes the library searchable, and the trend acquisition lanes pull in external trend signal. The QuickSearch job layer joins the two at request time.

Figure 1: High-level architecture.

The system has three parts that run on independent schedules. Two acquire and structure information. The third resolves a user’s single selection into a multi-stage retrieval operation across both.

It has been revealed that this pipeline makes the library legible. It works asynchronously on ingest. An AWS Step Functions state machine orchestrates roughly two dozen Python AWS Lambda functions end to end. The following steps trace one video from upload to indexed clips.

The pipeline is event-driven end to end. Every Lambda task retries with exponential backoff. The scene-description stage adds a dedicated throttling retry with full jitter. Non-critical enrichment steps degrade gracefully rather than failing the run, and a hard failure routes to an error handler that records the reason and reports the asset as failed.

In a recent development, same-Region staging for Marengo. Marengo is available in a specific set of AWS Regions. Asynchronous invocation in Amazon Bedrock reads input from and writes output to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region as the endpoint. The pipeline is built around those parameters. It stages each video into a dedicated bucket in US East (N. Virginia) before invoking Marengo, then reads the embedding output back from the same bucket. The rest of the infrastructure stays in its home Region while each embedding job runs alongside the model. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

This pipeline operates continuously and independently of any library, and it is what makes Trend Align possible.

It has been revealed that quotable Quotes draws on a second, narrower input: an external dialogue popularity signal, used strictly to weight lines that have already circulated. It’s optional by design, so if the signal is unavailable a line gets no boost rather than failing the job.

It has been revealed that this layer is where a single selection becomes a retrieval strategy. It executes each action asynchronously and returns a ranked set of clips.

Three choices made culturally informed retrieval tractable.

Industry observers note that A library changes when newly introduced content is added. Trends change daily, and early-stage trends faster than that. Coupling the two would mean either reprocessing content against fresh signal, which is computationally untenable, or serving stale trend judgment. Keeping them as independent pipelines joined at request time means signal stays current without the library ever being touched again. A title that finished airing years ago can re-enter a live conversation.

The naive design puts one large model in front of the whole library. QuickSearch instead uses inexpensive, high-recall vector and keyword retrieval to build a candidate pool, then spends model budget only on ranking a capped set of real candidates. The caps are sized against the ranking model’s output token limit, because a ranker that truncates mid-response silently drops results. This also keeps the per-query cost of Amazon Bedrock predictable: one embedding call, one rerank call, and a small fixed number of Claude invocations, regardless of library size.

Recent findings suggest that results are cached for 30 days. Without intervention, a change to an action’s criteria or model would stay invisible to people until the cache expired. Each action carries a pipeline version that is bumped in the same change that alters its behavior. That bump invalidates prior results immediately, so editorial judgment is refined as a versioned change to the product rather than relitigated on every query.

Sources indicate that social Department reports the following outcomes from customer use of QuickSearch. These are the tech giant’s own observations rather than a controlled benchmark.

Sources indicate that “The hard part here was never the search. It was working out what to search for: how you take something a great marketer does on instinct, about which moment lands and why, and turn it into criteria a system can execute a thousand times. We spent a long time on that. Working with TrackIt on a compressed timeline, we went from spec to a live demo at NAB. TwelveLabs gives us the intelligence to understand what’s inside the footage and AWS gives us the infrastructure to do it at library scale. Our job is to know what to point it at.”.

— Jonathan Verk, Founder and CEO, Social Department.

Industry observers note that “Everyone in media talks about adding metadata to their libraries but tagging content doesn’t pay for itself. What I like about this project is that it closes the loop. It takes reveals sitting in an archive and makes them useful for real campaigns, at a cost that makes sense to run every day. That’s the part the industry has been missing.”.

— Chris Marchitelli, Vice President, TrackIt.

The following four lessons from the project stood out.

Retrieval is largely solved. What isn’t solved is specifying intent precisely enough for retrieval to be useful without an expert marketer in the loop. Most of the engineering effort went into defining what qualifies as a shareable scene or a memeable frame, tightly enough to execute repeatedly across libraries with different tones and audiences. That definition is the output of a standing evaluation program of numbered iterations, each measured against per-show ground-truth sets and a tracked baseline, that tunes the criteria against results rather than intuition.

It has been revealed that quickSearch uses a multi-model architecture, with each model assigned to the work it fits best. Claude Haiku handles bounded, cost-sensitive output, and Claude Sonnet handles tasks where cultural recall changes the answer. TwelveLabs Marengo produces multimodal embeddings, TwelveLabs Pegasus provides scene-level video reasoning, and the Amazon Rerank model handles reranking. Amazon Bedrock made this architecture practical to build and run. Models from TwelveLabs, Anthropic, and Amazon are available through one API, so Social Department can change the model behind a task when measured quality moves, without building a new integration. Asynchronous invocation runs long video embedding jobs at library scale, and the Rerank API adds a relevance pass without separately hosted infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen search input in the same service, and customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. Because Amazon Bedrock is fully managed, the team operates no model-serving infrastructure of its own.

In a recent development, treating trend data as another input to the content pipeline would have failed, because the two have incompatible lifecycles. Recognizing early that library content and live culture are separate systems, with separate refresh rates, storage, and failure modes, was the decision the rest of the design depended on.

Social Department owned the pipeline architecture, retrieval system, and editorial criteria. TrackIt built and delivered against that architecture, and TwelveLabs supplied the video understanding models. AWS, with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, provided the infrastructure, model access, and solution architecture for the AWS components. Because each party had a clearly defined scope, the 8-week production timeline held.

In a recent development, we described how Social Department, working with TrackIt, TwelveLabs, and AWS, built culture-aware video discovery for entertainment marketing using its own pipeline and retrieval architecture. Several AWS components make up the layer this post describes. TwelveLabs Marengo handles multimodal embedding and TwelveLabs Pegasus handles scene-level video reasoning, both on Amazon Bedrock. Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock handle interpretation and editorial ranking, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless handles hybrid retrieval. AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, AWS Elemental MediaConvert, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon SQS run the pipelines around them. The result is a set of single-action queries that return the clips audiences already care about, the lines they already quote, the frames that will work as memes, and the moments that connect to whatever is trending right now.

Industry observers note that to get started with multimodal video understanding on AWS, explore Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. To learn more about the TwelveLabs models available on Amazon Bedrock, visit the TwelveLabs page on AWS Marketplace. To explore how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center can help your organization, visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center page.

Acknowledgements: The authors would like to thank Katie Kenney, Pranay Duhan, Xiaoye Qian, Rinne Han, and Dahler Battle for their work on this solution. We would also like to thank the TrackIt and TwelveLabs teams for their support.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:.

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

Sources indicate that the UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

It has been revealed that figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

It has been revealed that A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

According to recent reports, we will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Industry observers note that figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

According to recent reports, with the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:.

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:.

Sample prompt used in this example:.

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Sample prompt used in this example:.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’.

Industry observers note that the full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

View CSAF Summary meta-iot2050 (https://github.com/siemens/meta-iot2050) from V01.03.01 contains a Command Injection vulnerability in the firmware update tool that could allow an attacker which is able to manipulate a configuration file to have arbitrary commands run as root. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. The following versions of Siemens meta-iot2050 are affected: meta-iot2050 vers:intdot/>=01.03.01 (CVE-2026-109830) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.3 Siemens meta-iot2050 1 Vulnerability Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection') Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Tech giant Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109830 Affected devices take parts from a configuration file and execute them unchecked. This could allow an attacker which is able to manipulate the configuration file to make the user execute arbitrary code on the device. Read More 1 Affected Product meta-iot2050 >= V01.03.01 Product Status: known_affected Remediations None availableCurrently no fix is available Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-78 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection') CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.3 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends customers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. #3405. How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2821 w)

How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI.
  • It has been revealed that salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions.
  • Recent findings suggest that this post shows how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI.

It has been revealed that salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions. These include both models trained in house and open source models. Hosting models separately in each Region splits capacity and makes traffic spikes harder to absorb, which turns a capacity shortfall into an availability problem.

Recent findings suggest that this post shows how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments. It also walks through how Salesforce sees where each request was served and why. The cross-Region inference routing gives an application one invocation path across SageMaker AI endpoints in several Regions and accounts, and sends each request to an endpoint that can serve it. Those endpoints are Salesforce’s own, already deployed. The post starts with the capacity problem Salesforce faced, explains how the router works and how Salesforce integrated it into its Internal Gateway, walks through an example setup, and then describes what the team observed.

According to recent reports, salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves customers from the Region their requests come from, across 30+ global Regions and hundreds of AWS accounts, and they provision capacity based on each customer’s traffic. Every customer has its own peak window, and those windows often overlap. Provisioning for the overlapping peak would be the safe choice, but it costs too much. Customers also onboard new business units at short notice, so they must grow the fleet quickly. Adding capacity quickly, Region by Region, leaves Salesforce with capacity fragmentation: some Regions have idle instances while others run out.

Before the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, Salesforce used its Internal Gateway to send traffic that the local endpoints couldn’t handle to other Regions. The team built and operated this path, supported by basic health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic. That approach had two gaps. First, the gateway had no capacity signals from either the local or the remote endpoint, so it couldn’t tell when to shift traffic or whether the destination had room. Second, cross-Region traffic had to leave the virtual private cloud (VPC) through a NAT gateway and an internet gateway and travel over public AWS networking. In design reviews, the team also raised the risk of cascading failures: moving traffic during an incident can overload the next Region, so Salesforce needed a cap on cross-Region traffic.

Building this logic separately in every application doesn’t scale across Salesforce. The team needed a managed, capacity-aware routing path.

The inference router is a Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account. Your application invokes the router instead of an endpoint, passing a routing target name with the same request body and content type it sends to InvokeEndpoint today. A routing target is a name you choose for one logical model, such as a toxicity classifier, and it lists the endpoints and inference components that may serve that model by their full Amazon Resource Names (ARNs). A router holds one routing target per model, and a problem with one model’s endpoints does not move traffic for the others. A routing target can mix single-model endpoints and inference components.

Recent findings suggest that because each destination is named by its ARN, it can be in another Region or another AWS account. The account that owns an endpoint grants access through a resource-based endpoint policy that allows one named router to invoke it, which is how Salesforce runs it.

The router prefers its own Region, and while the local destination serves successfully, requests stay there. The router judges each destination by the outcomes of recent requests. Platform faults, 5xx errors from the model container, throttles, and timeouts lower a destination’s health. As they persist, the router moves a growing share of new requests to healthy destinations, typically starting within about a minute. It can take several minutes for a destination with little traffic. Signals such as scaling progress and failed instance introduces affect how swiftly the router responds once errors appear, but they do not move traffic by themselves. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left, so it does not swing back and forth. When a destination fails a request without running the model, for example by throttling it, the router retries that request once on another destination.

Recent findings suggest that client errors such as invalid input do not move traffic, because they would fail the same way in any Region. Model latency does not move traffic either, because a slow response often reflects a long prompt or output and does not by itself mean the endpoint is unhealthy. The router also does not deploy models, copy artifacts, or add instances. It uses the capacity you have deployed, and each endpoint’s own autoscaling keeps adding instances as its traffic grows.

In Salesforce’s Internal Gateway, the router call sits exactly where the direct InvokeEndpoint call used to be: in the per-request egress path, after the data residency check and before response handling. That check is the one routing decision the gateway keeps. A request tagged with a residency requirement is pinned to its in-Region routing target, whose only destination is the local endpoint, so it can never fail over across a boundary. Everything else goes to the router with the same body, content type, and accept type the gateway already sent. Capacity awareness, health assessment, and failover now live in the routing layer instead of in Salesforce’s code.

Figure 1: End-to-end architecture for cross-Region inference routing at Salesforce. In each Region, the Internal Gateway sends client requests through a VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink). Requests with the data residency flag set to true go directly to the in-Region Endpoint A and never leave their Region. All other requests go to the local inference router, which sends traffic to its local Endpoint A by default and fails over to Endpoint A in another Region when the local endpoint highlights signs of capacity constraints.

Salesforce treats the two routing fields on every response as first-class telemetry. The gateway logs InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason on the same structured line as the existing request ID and trace ID, and emits them as application performance monitoring (APM) tags. Because the ARN carries the Region and account, a single log line demonstrates whether a request ran locally or crossed a boundary, and why: local-preferred, failover, capacity-available, or only-healthy. The team joins these fields against the router’s Amazon CloudWatch metrics when investigating a traffic shift.

The gateway’s timeout accounts for cross-Region round-trip latency, so a request that fails over has time to complete in the remote Region. Because the router already retries once on another destination, the gateway adds no retries of its own, which keeps attempts from multiplying during an incident.

Industry observers note that the following walkthrough demonstrates the configuration Salesforce tested, using example IDs and names. Salesforce first created a router in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) with a local destination and confirmed that requests were routed to it. The team then registered an endpoint in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2) owned by a different account, removed the local destination, and confirmed that requests reached the remote endpoint across the account and Region boundary. In the examples, the router account is 111122223333, and the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint is 444455556666.

In the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, with a condition that limits access to one named router. The router does not need to exist yet, so you can use the ARN of the router you strategy to create.

The sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition means the router account can reach the endpoint only through that router. The endpoint owner can revoke access at any time with delete-endpoint-policy.

In the router account, create the router in us-west-2 with one routing target that lists both destinations by ARN.

Each additional model becomes another entry in RoutingTargets.

In a recent development, before sending traffic, call DescribeInferenceRouter and check each destination’s RoutingStatus. Routable means SageMaker AI could read the destination and it can serve traffic. Unroutable means the destination was read but can’t serve right now, for example because the endpoint is not InService. Unknown means SageMaker AI couldn’t read the destination with your credentials, for example because you lack sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint (or sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent for an inference component), or, for a destination in another account, because its endpoint policy doesn’t grant Describe.

The change in the calling code is small. The request body, content type, and accept type stay exactly as they were. The client and operation change, and the endpoint name is replaced by the router name and the routing target name.

An InferenceId and CustomAttributes are passed through to the destination as with InvokeEndpoint, so identifiers such as a trace ID travel with the request. Members such as TargetVariant and InferenceComponentName are not used, because the routing target replaces them.

In a recent development, most teams evaluating a routing layer first ask how to tell what it did. The inference router answers on every response and in Amazon CloudWatch. Each response carries the ARN of the destination that served it and a routing reason, in the InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields and in the matching X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routed-Resource-Arn and X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routing-Reason headers. Because the ARN includes the Region and account, logging both values with your own request logs gives you a per-request record of whether each call ran locally or crossed a boundary.

The routing reason takes one of four values. local-preferred means a healthy destination in the router’s Region served the request. failover means a destination in the router’s Region exists but isn’t serving reliably, so the router sent the request elsewhere. capacity-available means no destination in the router’s Region could take the request, and it went to one of several healthy destinations in other Regions. only-healthy means it was served by the only eligible destination that was healthy.

According to recent reports, in aggregate, the router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, each carrying the router name and destination ARN, so the cross-Region picture is visible from one place. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations counts requests per destination, and its error.type attribute splits failures into invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx (including timeouts), and invocation_model_error for errors returned by the model.

In a recent development, aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration measures the time each destination took, and aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration measures the time the router added, including the network to and from a remote Region. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status reports each destination’s health state as healthy, overloaded, or degraded. You query these metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch Query Studio, and you can place them next to each endpoint’s existing SageMaker AI metrics on a cross-account, cross-Region dashboard.

Figure 2: CloudWatch dashboard during a failover test run by AWS with a test model. Requests per destination shift from the local us-east-2 endpoint to endpoints in us-west-2 as the local destination becomes degraded, then return gradually after recovery.

It has been revealed that salesforce tested the router in two configurations. First, same-Region routing in us-west-2, where the Internal Gateway called the local inference router and the router sent requests to the local Endpoint A. Second, cross-account, cross-Region routing, where the router in us-west-2 also listed an endpoint in us-east-2 owned by a separate infrastructure account. Before sending traffic, the team called DescribeInferenceRouter and confirmed that the routing target listed both destinations and that both reported a RoutingStatus of Routable. Requests sent to the router were then served by the local endpoint, with a routing reason of local-preferred. Setup took little effort: the endpoint owner added an endpoint policy for the router’s account, and the router call replaced the direct InvokeEndpoint call in the gateway’s egress path, with the same request body, content type, and accept type.

To test failover, the team flooded the local endpoint in us-west-2 until it was saturated, while a separate probe kept invoking the router and recorded where each request was served and how long it took. For about five minutes of saturation, probe latency at p50 rose from 0.2 seconds to 45 to 58 seconds, and traffic stayed in us-west-2. This is the intended behavior, because latency alone does not move traffic. When requests began to exceed the model container’s 60-second handler timeout and return errors, the router started to shift traffic. The first requests reached us-east-2 about two minutes after the first errors, and within another minute about 78 percent of probe traffic was served in us-east-2. The remaining 20 to 25 percent stayed local so the router could detect recovery.

Sources indicate that once traffic had moved, p50 latency returned to 0.2 seconds, and the cross-Region path added under 100 milliseconds at p50. After the local endpoint recovered, traffic returned to us-west-2 gradually over about 10 minutes, and the probe recorded no errors during failover or failback. The InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields on each response, together with the router’s per-destination invocation metrics in CloudWatch, demonstrated the whole sequence without any extra instrumentation.

Sources indicate that figure 3: Share of probe requests by Region during the Salesforce failover test (UTC). Traffic stays in us-west-2 while the local endpoint is saturated, shifts to us-east-2 once requests begin returning errors (peaking at about 78 percent), then returns gradually to us-west-2 over about 10 minutes after recovery.

The router lets Salesforce replace operational logic the team used to build and run itself: the health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic in the Internal Gateway. Capacity signals and failover now live in the routing layer, not in each application.

Before broader adoption, Salesforce intends to repeat the failover test with the local endpoint held at saturation for longer, measure cross-Region latency at millisecond precision, evaluate cascading-Region behavior at the cross-Region cap, and roll out the router across more Regions.

Sources indicate that “With the upcoming cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI, we can add capacity securely and keep our data residency commitments. Workloads that must stay in a region stay there, and only eligible traffic can be served from another Region. A single managed call works alongside our existing failover logic, so we didn’t have to re-architect our application or change our payloads. SageMaker AI handles routing, health detection, and fallback, and customer data always stays within the Salesforce trust boundary. We decide which Regions are eligible and control access through endpoint policies that we own. Because inference router works with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail, we also get a complete observability, cost-tracking, and governance architecture for our workloads.”.

— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce.

Keep the same model, container image, and artifacts available in every Region you register, because the router does not copy them, and a destination that runs a different model version will return different answers to the same request.

In a recent development, size each destination Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you expect to send it. The router does not create capacity, and if every eligible destination is busy, your application receives the destinations’ own errors. Configure autoscaling on each destination the way you do today, with enough headroom that a receiving endpoint can scale out under its own policy when traffic arrives from another Region.

Customers can set the cap in the receiving endpoint’s configuration (CrossRegionTrafficConfig), as a per-instance request rate and the largest share of the endpoint’s capacity that remote traffic may use. Local traffic never counts against the cap. When remote traffic reaches it, the endpoint stops accepting additional requests from other Regions and the router sends them to other destinations, so local callers keep their capacity. The cap applies to real-time endpoints.

Sources indicate that salesforce serves a wide variety of models for products across the firm in 30+ global Regions, and hosting them separately in each Region had turned capacity shortfalls into availability problems. With the inference router, Salesforce registers the endpoints it already runs in different Regions and accounts behind one call, so traffic that a local endpoint cannot serve reaches capacity elsewhere instead of failing. Requests that must stay in a Region stay there, endpoint owners authorize cross-account access through policies they control, and every response reveals where a request ran and why. SageMaker AI handles the routing, health assessment, and gradual return of traffic after recovery, instead of each calling application building that logic itself. This lets Salesforce add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments.

The cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI is generally available starting November 18, 2026, in all commercial Regions where inference is supported for real-time endpoints. To get started, see the Inference router documentation in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide and the CreateInferenceRouter API reference.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21479v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

Tech Report: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run.
  • Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.
  • Industry observers note that the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

Industry observers note that the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise prepares include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

According to recent reports, the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million people, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

According to recent reports, when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the newly introduced routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

Sources indicate that routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

In a recent development, pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two fresh tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics indicates the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

Sources indicate that in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

According to recent reports, this is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#3399. Tech Report: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (320 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (320 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21001v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that many teams that build applications self-host their identity provider (IdP), such as Keycloak or PingFederate, inside a private network.
  • AgentCore Identity now supports private CA certificates for private identity providers.
  • It has been revealed that in this post, we show you how to issue an IdP certificate with AWS Private Certificate Authority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that many teams that build applications self-host their identity provider (IdP), such as Keycloak or PingFederate, inside a private network. These IdPs usually present a TLS server certificate from a private certificate authority (CA). With private CA support in AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, your agents can now connect to these IdPs while trusting the private CA that your organization already uses.

AgentCore Identity now supports private CA certificates for private identity providers. You store the PEM-encoded CA certificate in AWS Secrets Manager or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference it from your credential provider. The CA certificate contains only the public certificate, not its private key. AgentCore Identity uses it to validate the server certificate presented by your IdP’s discovery, JSON Web Key Set (JWKS), and token endpoints. The CA certificate must be a root or intermediate CA certificate.

It has been revealed that in this post, we show you how to issue an IdP certificate with AWS Private Certificate Authority. We then configure an AgentCore Identity credential provider to trust it and rotate the CA while minimizing downtime. We also show how to protect the CA certificate so that only your IdP team can change it. Although AgentCore Identity supports any private CA, including enterprise, third-party, and self-signed root CAs, the walkthrough in this post uses AWS Private CA and Keycloak as the IdP.

According to recent reports, consider an agent that needs to call an internal wiki API protected by your Keycloak IdP. The agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which hosts your agent code. To get an OAuth 2.0 access token from Keycloak, the agent uses an AgentCore Identity credential provider, which holds the IdP connection details and client credentials.

Industry observers note that the following diagram shows this setup. Keycloak runs in your virtual private cloud (VPC) behind an internal Application Load Balancer. The load balancer presents an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) private certificate signed by AWS Private CA. The CA certificate that AgentCore Identity trusts is stored in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3.

Sources indicate that agentCore Identity reaches the IdP privately through Amazon VPC Lattice, which connects to your VPC through a resource gateway, an entry point for VPC Lattice traffic into your VPC. VPC Lattice is required for private CA support. If you choose the managed option, AgentCore Identity creates and manages the VPC Lattice resources for you.

Figure 1: Connecting AgentCore Identity to a self-hosted IdP that uses a private CA.

Agents that use machine-to-machine, on-behalf-of, and user-delegated flows can also use the private CA without changing their code.

To follow this walkthrough, you need:.

Keep the following in mind when you initiative your deployment:.

Industry observers note that the walkthrough has four steps. If your IdP already presents a certificate from your enterprise CA, skip to Step 2.

Start by creating a root CA in AWS Private CA. For instructions, see Create a private CA and Install the CA certificate. Choose general-purpose mode, because short-lived certificate mode concerns certificates that are valid for 7 days or less. When you create the CA, authorize ACM to renew certificates, so that ACM can renew the IdP’s server certificate before it expires.

Next, request the server certificate. AgentCore Identity checks that the certificate matches the IdP hostname, so include each hostname that appears in your IdP’s discovery document as a subject alternative name (SAN). In most Keycloak deployments, the discovery, JWKS, and token endpoints share one hostname. For example, if your discovery URL is https://keycloak.example.local/realms/agents/.well-known/openid-configuration, add keycloak.example.local as a SAN.

To request a private certificate for the IdP (console).

AgentCore Identity needs to trust the CA certificate to validate the IdP’s server certificate. Because it trusts the CA rather than the server certificate itself, you don’t need to update the credential provider each time the server certificate renews.

Export the CA certificate from AWS Private CA in PEM format:.

Before you upload the file, check it against the requirements. The file must be PEM-encoded and meet size requirements, containing only CA certificates that are within their validity period. The following commands show the CA flag, expiry date, and file size. The last command confirms that the IdP’s certificate chains to this CA. Run it from a host that can reach the IdP. It returns Verify return code: 0 (ok) when the chain is valid.

The output looks similar to the following:.

Store the file in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3. A Secrets Manager secret must be a string secret in the same account as the credential provider. An S3 object can be in another account, which suits organizations that run the IdP in a central account.

Give write access to the secret or object only to the team that operates your IdP. For an example policy, see Protect the CA certificate later in this post.

You can create the credential provider in the AgentCore console or with the AWS CLI. The private CA settings appear on the console only after you connect the OAuth client to a VPC, because private CA support applies only to private IdPs.

To create a credential provider that trusts your private CA (console).

The Root certificate authority field accepts either a root or an intermediate CA certificate.

Figure 2: Adding a root certificate from AWS Secrets Manager.

To create the same credential provider with the AWS CLI, add certificateConfigurations to the custom OAuth 2.0 provider configuration:.

To use Amazon S3 instead, replace the certificateConfigurations entry with {"s3": {"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/trust-anchors/keycloak-root-ca.pem", "bucketOwnerAccountId": "444455556666"}}. If you leave out bucketOwnerAccountId, AgentCore Identity expects the bucket to be in your own account. To keep the client secret out of your shell history, you can reference a client secret that you store in Secrets Manager.

It has been revealed that agentCore Identity validates the certificate and sets up private connectivity in the background, so a fresh credential provider starts in the CREATING status. Check the status after a few minutes:.

Recent findings suggest that on the console, the credential provider’s details page shows the configured certificate under Root certificates. When the status is READY, your agents can request tokens from the IdP. If the status is CREATE_FAILED, the failureReason field explains why. For example, Leaf certificates are not allowed, must provide CA certificates only means that you uploaded the server certificate instead of the CA certificate. If you see Unable to access S3 object or Secrets Manager can't find the specified secret, check that the URI or Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is correct. Also confirm that your identity can read the object or secret. If the provider is READY but token requests fail, confirm that the IdP’s server certificate was issued by the configured CA and has a SAN that matches the IdP hostname.

Recent findings suggest that after you verify that the credential provider trusts the private CA, monitor the CA certificate’s expiration and rotate it before it expires to prevent token request failures. AgentCore Identity publishes the EarliestCertificateDaysToExpiry metric to Amazon CloudWatch in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace when your agents request tokens through a credential provider that uses a private CA. The metric reports the days remaining until the earliest certificate in your PEM file expires. It has ProviderName, ProviderArn, and TokenVault dimensions. When you create an alarm, specify all three. We recommend a CloudWatch alarm that notifies you well before the value reaches zero, because token requests to the IdP stop working when the CA certificate expires.

In a recent development, NOTE: AgentCore Identity reads the certificate only when you create or update the credential provider. If you change the secret or S3 object, call UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider afterward so that AgentCore Identity reads the new content. Include certificateConfigurations in the update request. If you leave it out, the credential provider stops trusting your private CA.

According to recent reports, A PEM file can contain more than one CA certificate and AgentCore Identity trusts each of them. You can use this to rotate to a upcoming CA while minimizing downtime:.

In a recent development, agentCore Identity doesn’t check certificate revocation lists (CRLs) or use the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP). This means that if an unauthorized party obtains the private key for an IdP server certificate, AgentCore Identity continues to trust that certificate. This trust lasts until the certificate expires or until you stop trusting the CA that issued it. To stop trusting a CA, remove it from the PEM file and update the credential provider.

Industry observers note that A CA certificate contains no private key and is public by design, because you hand it to every client that has to trust your IdP. What you need to protect is the data integrity of the trust store, meaning the secret or S3 object that holds the certificate. If someone replaces the certificate or adds another CA certificate to the trust store, the next update could let an unauthorized party who can redirect traffic impersonate your IdP.

Industry observers note that we recommend that you scope permissions around writes rather than reads. Give write access, such as s3:PutObject or secretsmanager:PutSecretValue, only to the team or pipeline that operates the IdP. Give read access to the principals that call CreateOauth2CredentialProvider or UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider. During these operations, AgentCore Identity reads the CA certificate using the caller’s IAM permissions. The following bucket policy for a central identity account (444455556666) lets only the role that manages credential providers in a workload account (111122223333) read the CA certificates. It also requires that role to belong to your organization in AWS Organizations, and it denies writes from principals other than the IdP administrator role:.

Industry observers note that the principal in the workload account also needs s3:GetObject in its own IAM policy. For Secrets Manager, which must be in the same account, use a resource-based policy on the secret to restrict writes to the IdP administrator role.

Because the secret is in the same account, IAM policies can grant read access, so the resource policy only needs to deny changes:.

Turn on S3 Versioning to recover an overwritten file and AWS CloudTrail data events to record each change. Because the CA certificate isn’t confidential, SSE-S3 encryption is sufficient and avoids the cross-account AWS KMS permissions that a customer managed key requires.

According to recent reports, keep the trust scope of each credential provider narrow. Upload only the CA that concerns your IdP’s server certificate, rather than your organization’s full trust bundle. If your IdPs use different CAs, store each CA certificate in its own secret or S3 object so that each credential provider trusts only the CA that it needs.

You can also use a private CA for inbound authorization. When AgentCore Runtime or AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by a private IdP, it fetches the IdP’s discovery document and its signing keys from the JWKS endpoint. AgentCore Gateway validates the discovery URL when you create the gateway. If the CA certificate is missing or doesn’t match the IdP’s certificate chain, the gateway status changes to FAILED with the reason Failed to validate discovery url. To trust a private CA for that connection, add certificateConfigurations to the customJWTAuthorizer configuration, next to the existing privateEndpoint:.

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources that you created:.

In this post, we revealed how to connect AgentCore Identity to a self-hosted IdP that uses a certificate from your own CA. You issued a server certificate with AWS Private CA, stored the CA certificate in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3 and referenced it from a credential provider. You also saw how to rotate the CA with a combined PEM file and how to limit who can change the certificate that your agents trust.

In a recent development, to learn more, see Connect to private identity providers in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. For examples using Keycloak, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

View CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released fresh versions for several affected products and recommends to upgrade to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens products. Siemens has released newly introduced versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (172 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20827v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When processor implementation details are unavailable, black-box microarchitectural reverse engineering helps security researchers identify hardware conditions related to security vulnerabilities. However, this process requires substantial manual effort to design experiments, develop test programs, and analyze results for each processor. We present ProcReverser, a multi-agent system that automates this process. ProcReverser uses execution feedback to improve experimental intends and test programs and identifies microarchitectural properties from measurements. We develop a comprehensive suite of property identification tasks focused on hardware mechanisms relevant to Spectre-class attacks, covering speculative execution, branch prediction, memory dependence, and cache behavior. We evaluate ProcReverser on the XuanTie C910, the gem5 RISC-V O3 CPU model, and the SiFive P550. ProcReverser achieves Pass@1 and Pass@5 scores of 81.3% and 93.8%, respectively, on C910, and 83.0% and 100.0% on gem5 O3. On the SiFive P550, ProcReverser further characterizes microarchitectural properties covered by the proposed task suite. These findings highlight the potential of automated microarchitectural reverse engineering to support processor vulnerability analysis and defense evaluation.

Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Sources indicate that rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

Industry observers note that to find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

In a recent development, on-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

Sources indicate that on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

Industry observers note that we're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (334 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
